author: A Robot
objectives: Describe Mars’s apparent eastward drift, westward loop (retrograde), and return to eastward motion during a retrograde episode.
Explain apparent retrograde motion in the heliocentric model as a consequence of Earth overtaking a slower-moving outer planet.
Contrast geocentric versus heliocentric explanations and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred on grounds of parsimony.
Predict likely timing/geometry of retrograde for a given outer planet using relative orbital speed and phase geometry.
Compare retrograde loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and explain why more distant planets produce smaller loops.

modules.moduleName: Scene 1 — Earth’s View: Tracking Mars Night-to-Night
modules.description: Students observe Mars’s apparent motion relative to background stars over time, including slowing, reversal, looping, and resumption of eastward drift.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Identify the components of Mars’s apparent path: eastward drift, retrograde loop (westward motion), and return to eastward motion.
Explain that the observed change is apparent sky motion driven by changing relative geometry, not a literal reversal of Mars’s orbit direction.
instructions: Follow the Mars marker as its position updates across ‘nights’.
Watch for the point where the marker reverses direction, forming a loop.

components.text: Earth’s view: track Mars against fixed stars

clips.changeMeaning: Scene 1 begins with a fixed star field and a labeled Mars marker. A small trail node appears to anchor the first ‘night’ measurement so students can compare subsequent apparent positions.
clips.narration: In this scene you’ll track Mars the way you would from Earth: against a background of stars. Mars drifts eastward, slows, reverses into retrograde westward motion, traces a loop, and then resumes eastward drift.

clips.changeMeaning: The Mars marker shifts slightly rightward (eastward) while the trail node updates to the new apparent position. This models successive nights and emphasizes a gradual eastward drift.
clips.narration: Over the next several nights, Mars moves a little eastward relative to the background stars. Its true space motion is steady, but the apparent direction changes across time.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars still advances eastward, but the visual step size is smaller and the marker grows slightly to signal the approach to the reversal. Students see ‘slowing down’ just before retrograde begins.
clips.narration: As retrograde approaches, Mars appears to slow. You can picture it as smaller eastward steps night after night.

clips.changeMeaning: The marker shifts back leftward, marking the start of retrograde motion. The color change highlights that the apparent direction to Mars has switched from east to west.
clips.narration: Then Mars reverses. Apparent westward motion begins—that’s the retrograde part of the loop.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars continues westward and begins to curve, creating the visual ‘loop’ trajectory in apparent sky position. The updated marker and trail node show that retrograde is more than a simple one-step reversal.
clips.narration: During retrograde, Mars doesn’t just move westward—it traces a loop across the constellations.

clips.changeMeaning: The marker moves back toward the earlier eastward positions, ending the retrograde interval. Returning the original color reinforces that the loop phase has completed.
clips.narration: Finally, Mars slows again and resumes eastward drift. That completes the loop pattern you’d observe over weeks and months.

modules.moduleName: Scene 2 — Heliocentric Explanation: Earth Overtakes Mars
modules.description: Students switch to a Sun-centered perspective with Earth’s faster inner orbit overtaking Mars’s slower outer orbit, producing the apparent loop from relative motion.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain retrograde as a consequence of different orbital angular speeds: Earth moves faster in its inner orbit than Mars.
Connect the appearance of reversal/loop to changing relative geometry (relative angular separation), not to a true reversal in Mars’s orbit direction.
instructions: Observe the relative motion: the inner (Earth) orbit sweeps ahead of the outer (Mars) orbit.
Watch how the spatial configuration corresponds to retrograde from Earth’s viewpoint.

components.text: Earth orbits faster (inner orbit) → overtakes Mars
Loop is apparent: relative motion changes the sky direction

clips.changeMeaning: Establishes the outside, heliocentric viewpoint: Sun at the center, tilted orbit rings, and Earth and Mars at starting positions. Labels cue the key idea—relative orbital speed and overtaking.
clips.narration: Now switch perspectives to outside the solar system. Earth orbits faster on its smaller inner path than Mars does on its larger outer path. When Earth overtakes Mars, Mars traces a loop in the sky as seen from Earth.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth advances further along its inner orbit while Mars lags behind. The updated positions represent the changing heliocentric phase that later produces retrograde from the Earth’s line of sight.
clips.narration: As days pass, Earth moves ahead along its orbit while Mars changes position more slowly. Their relative angular separation on the sky evolves.

clips.changeMeaning: At near-overtake geometry, Earth passes ahead of Mars in heliocentric angle. Mars appears slightly larger to emphasize the critical moment where the apparent direction begins to swing backward (retrograde).
clips.narration: When Earth overtakes Mars, the direction from Earth toward Mars starts to swing backward. That signals the beginning of retrograde in the apparent loop.

clips.changeMeaning: After overtaking, Earth continues moving quickly while Mars remains slower, preserving the relative geometry that corresponds to the middle of the apparent loop. Students see smooth evolution rather than a sudden flip.
clips.narration: After the overtake, the relative geometry changes smoothly. From Earth, that maps into the curved, looping path across constellations.

clips.changeMeaning: The system moves away from the overtake configuration: Earth progresses further along the orbit so the net apparent motion returns to eastward (prograde). Mars returns to baseline size.
clips.narration: Eventually Earth moves past Mars in heliocentric angle, and the apparent direction to Mars switches back to eastward drift. Retrograde ends.

modules.moduleName: Scene 3 — Geocentric vs Heliocentric: Why Parallax Loop Matters
modules.description: Students compare geocentric and heliocentric explanations using side-by-side text cards and a rotating epicycle concept versus a simpler relative-motion glyph.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe how heliocentric explanations reduce the need for multiple adjustable epicycles to match the retrograde observation.
Explain retrograde as an apparent effect of viewing geometry and relative speeds, not an actual reversal of Mars’s orbital motion.
instructions: Compare the ‘extra circles’ idea in the geocentric card against the single coherent mechanism in the heliocentric card.
Use the central marker as a reminder that both models must match the same observational data.

components.text:
Geocentric model (Earth center)
Retrograde needs epicycles

Heliocentric model (Sun center)
Loop emerges from relative orbits

clips.changeMeaning: Presents side-by-side conceptual representations: geocentric epicycles and a heliocentric relative-motion glyph. The central observation marker indicates the single data pattern retrograde must match.
clips.narration: Both models aim to match the same observation: Mars traces a loop. But they do it differently. Geocentric explanations use extra constructs—epicycles—while heliocentric explanations use relative orbital motion.

clips.changeMeaning: Emphasizes the geocentric mechanism by scaling and rotating the epicycle system. The observation marker color shifts to signal increased ‘complexity’ in the geocentric fit.
clips.narration: In a geocentric framework, reproducing retrograde typically means adding epicycles and fine-tuning their parameters—an extra layer of complexity.

clips.changeMeaning: De-emphasizes epicycles while emphasizing the relative-motion glyph. The observation marker shifts and turns green, reinforcing that heliocentrism accounts for the loop without extra constructs.
clips.narration: In heliocentrism, the same loop appears naturally. Earth’s faster inner orbit relative to Mars produces the apparent reversal and loop without needing additional epicycles.

clips.changeMeaning: Final emphasis keeps both cards readable while the green observation marker highlights the key concept: retrograde is apparent and emerges from geometry and relative speed.
clips.narration: Key takeaway: retrograde motion is apparent. The heliocentric model attributes it to geometry and relative speeds—one coherent mechanism rather than multiple nested epicycles.

modules.moduleName: Scene 4 — Compare Mars, Jupiter, Saturn Loops (Why Loops Differ)
modules.description: Students compare the apparent retrograde loop size for Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn and connect smaller loops to smaller relative-motion effects for more distant planets.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Compare loop amplitude among Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.
Explain qualitatively why more distant planets produce smaller apparent retrograde loops.
Predict loop-size ordering for outer planets based on relative orbital speed differences.
instructions: Look at the loop-size markers: larger loop indicates stronger relative-motion effect.
Predict which planet has the largest loop among the three.

clips.changeMeaning: Introduces three parallel loop visualizations with decreasing sizes: Mars largest, Jupiter medium, Saturn smallest. An Earth-passing marker anchors the shared ‘overtaking’ idea across all three comparisons.
clips.narration: Retrograde loops occur for multiple outer planets. Compare their sizes: Mars has the largest apparent loop, Jupiter’s is smaller, and Saturn’s is smallest.

clips.changeMeaning: Focuses attention on Mars by scaling its loop larger and shrinking the others. The Earth-passing marker shifts toward the Mars column to connect ‘strongest relative effect’ with the overtaking geometry.
clips.narration: Why is Mars larger? Earth’s orbital speed difference relative to Mars is greatest among these planets, so the apparent loop is larger.

clips.changeMeaning: Swaps emphasis to Jupiter by increasing its loop size relative to Mars and leaving Saturn small. The Earth marker shifts slightly toward Jupiter to reinforce the relative-speed reasoning.
clips.narration: For Jupiter, the orbital-speed difference with Earth is smaller because Jupiter is farther from the Sun. The relative-motion effect decreases, so the loop shrinks.

clips.changeMeaning: Highlights Saturn’s smallest loop by scaling it up relative to the other two in the final comparison stage. The Earth marker aligns with Saturn’s column to complete the ordering explanation.
clips.narration: Saturn’s loop is smallest because it moves even more slowly in heliocentric angle relative to Earth. The overtaking geometry produces only a modest apparent reversal.
